lines.text: A small land in the heart of the Balkans, sacred to some and home to others, that fought its way to statehood. This is the story of Kosovo.
In the 1300s, when Kosovo was a heart of the medieval Serbian state, the monastery of Visoki Decani was built. It is now a World Heritage Site.
In 1389 Serbian and Ottoman armies met on the field of Kosovo. The Ottomans won in the end, and ruled here for more than four centuries.
In 1878 Albanian leaders gathered at Prizren and formed a league to defend their lands, the start of the Albanian national movement.
Ibrahim Rugova, a writer born in 1944, would lead the Albanians of Kosovo in peaceful resistance to Serbian rule, and become their president.
Albin Kurti, born in 1975, would be a student activist and later prime minister.
Vjosa Osmani, born in 1982, would become a lawyer and politician, and in 2021 the president of Kosovo.
In 1990 the singer Rita Ora was born in Pristina, one of many families who soon left the troubled land.
A year later came Majlinda Kelmendi, the judoka who would win Kosovo's first Olympic gold medal in 2016.
And in 1995 Dua Lipa was born in London to Kosovo Albanian parents. She grew up partly in Pristina before her rise to world fame.
In 1998 war broke out between Albanian fighters and the forces of Yugoslavia. Hundreds of thousands were driven from their homes.
In the spring of 1999 NATO bombed Yugoslavia for weeks, until its forces withdrew from Kosovo.
The United Nations then took over the running of Kosovo, a mission meant to bridge the years until its future was settled.
Alongside it came a NATO-led force, KFOR, which has kept the peace ever since.
In February 2008, after nearly a decade under international rule, Kosovo stepped forward as a state of its own.
Its parliament declared independence from Serbia. Many countries recognise it, but Serbia still does not.
Young, disputed and determined, Kosovo is still writing its own story in the Balkans.
